messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Patel, a 29-year-old painter, came to treatment months after being mugged on his way home from a residential job. He had stayed late finishing trim in a vacant apartment building, carrying his backpack with brushes, cash from the day, and his phone. In the dim stretch between the train stop and his car, two men came up fast from behind a wall. What he remembers most clearly is the scrape of shoes, one man grabbing his shoulder, and the flash of a hand near his face as they demanded his bag. Other parts feel broken off or missing. He has told the story several times to his wife, but each time he gets stuck on fragments and cannot deliberately pull the whole sequence together. When he does get close to the memory, what hits him is a sharp guilt that he should have seen them earlier, should have fought harder, should not have been carrying cash.

In the weeks after, Arjun tried to return to work as if nothing had changed. But waking from nightmares left a residue that stayed in his body long after morning. On those days he would arrive at job sites already tense, shoulders tight, jaw set, moving room to room as if someone might step out from behind a doorway. Passing the block near the mugging, or even entering an unfamiliar apartment complex for work, could bring the scene into his mind all at once. A hallway with poor lighting, footsteps echoing on concrete, or the sight of an alcove would make his body surge into readiness before he could think. He began scanning stairwells, parking lots, and windows automatically, and if a client approached him suddenly with a question he could snap back irritably, embarrassed by how quickly he turned sharp or angry.

These moments also pulled at the memory itself. A location resembling the one where he was attacked could force up a sudden image of being grabbed, while leaving the rest inaccessible, as if the worst second of it was vivid and everything around it had dropped away. He found this especially unnerving after nightmares: he would wake with his heart pounding and a sense that something terrible had just happened, then spend the morning with bits of the robbery intruding into his mind without being able to place them in order. The more these fragments came uninvited, the more certain he became that the memory held something he had failed to do. That guilt on recall hardened into a broader conclusion that people were not safe and that he had been foolish to assume otherwise.

Since the robbery, Arjun had come to believe that people cannot be trusted and that relying on anyone leaves you exposed. He said this was the part his wife did not understand: she wanted to reassure him, but reassurance from other people no longer felt usable to him. He kept thinking that no one had been there when it mattered, and that in the end he was on his own. That belief has left him feeling cut off even at home. He sits apart, answers briefly, and watches the street from the apartment window at night. Being around strangers now carries an expectation of danger, and that expectation keeps his body braced; in crowded stores or on jobs in unfamiliar neighborhoods he scans faces, exits, and blind corners continuously, becoming irritable if anyone tells him he is overreacting.

Those same beliefs have made the world feel full of reminders. Because he is certain other people may take advantage of him, any physical location where he lacks control—a parking garage, an empty corridor, a stairwell in a building he has been hired to paint—starts to feel charged before anything happens. He notices himself listening for footsteps, and once he begins looking, ordinary cues quickly become triggers. A stranger lingering by an entrance, voices behind him, or waking from a nightmare after sleeping lightly will set off not only the bodily tension but also the sudden return of the memory fragments. In turn, those fragments deepen his conviction that something essential was missed and that he cannot rely on anyone to keep him safe.

What has frightened Arjun most is how self-sustaining it has become. The more incomplete the memory feels, the more he searches his surroundings for danger, as if vigilance could prevent another blind spot; the more he lives in that state, the more easily places and dream residue ignite the same images again. His wife has begun urging him not to take evening jobs because he comes home edgy and distant, and he has turned down work in larger apartment buildings because he cannot tolerate enclosed hallways without feeling his body gear up. He finally sought help after waking from a nightmare and nearly shouting at his wife when she touched his shoulder to calm him. He said he is afraid that if this continues he will lose both his work and his marriage, and he hopes, cautiously, that he might stop feeling as if danger is waiting in every corner.
